subject: Biology
title: The Human Genome Project
description: One-minute skill: The Human Genome Project.

hook.text: In 1990, scientists launched a $3 billion effort to read every letter of the human genome.

buildup.text: Thousands of researchers in 20 countries worked together for 13 years to finish the map.

discovery.text: The project found about 20,000 genes—far fewer than the 100,000 scientists had predicted.

twist.text: Today, the same sequencing costs under $200 and takes a single day instead of 13 years.

climax.text: The genome map opened the door to personalized medicine, ancestry testing, and gene therapy.

punchline.text: Reading the book of life took 13 years. Now it takes a day.

quiz.question: How many genes did the Human Genome Project find?

details.summary: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year international effort completed in 2003 that sequenced the entire human genome for the first time. Costing about $2.7 billion, it created the reference genome that underpins modern genetics, genomics, and personalized medicine.
details.whyItMatters: The HGP transformed biology by providing a complete reference for all human genes. It drove sequencing technology costs down from billions to under $1,000 per genome, democratizing genetic research worldwide.
takeaways: The project ran from 1990 to 2003 as an international collaboration
It revealed humans have about 20,000 genes, far fewer than expected
Competition from Craig Venter's Celera accelerated the public project

faq.question: What were the biggest surprises from the Human Genome Project?
faq.answer: The low gene count of about 20,000 shocked scientists expecting far more. The vast amount of non-coding DNA was unexpected. And the degree of genetic similarity between humans and other species challenged assumptions about human genetic uniqueness.

faq.question: How has the Human Genome Project impacted medicine?
faq.answer: It enabled pharmacogenomics, genetic testing for thousands of conditions, cancer genomics that guides targeted therapy, and gene therapy development. The reference genome is used in virtually every biomedical research lab in the world today.
